title: CLO 2025 Academic Month  Sutured and Unsutured
description: CLO 2025 Official Academic Monthly Course Review is now online! Professor Catherine Andreozzi from Rhode Island School of Design and artist Joy Ko focus on stitched and unstitched materials, using students' fashion design works as a starting point to deeply explore the efficient results CLO brings to fashion design.
transcript:
I'd like to introduce myself. My name is Catherine Andreuzzi. I'm a full-time professor in the apparel design department at Rhode Island School of Design. We've put together a presentation that we also gave Joy and me. Joy is with me. You'll meet her later. She is a faculty member in the textiles department at RISD. We gave this presentation at the New York CLO Summit last fall and it was really well received, so we're very happy to do it again and we're happy to be asked. So we're going to take you through what we're calling stitched and unstitched. So, fittingly, I work with the stitched materials and Joy works with the unstitched. So I'm going to start the presentation with some of my apparel students' work. Right here we're looking at Alexandra Debler. She used CLO to design and develop her senior thesis collection inspired by the occult and tarot cards. Here's an example of intricate beading design she developed in CLO, depicting the phases of the moon on the back of the jacket.

Alex found a very clever way to use the animation feature in CLO and play it back and then freeze the animation when she found the appropriate movement of the cloth that she wanted to use. And then she would do her final rendering.

This is a render for a still image this way. This render has the model in a mid-stride, like I was talking about earlier. And you can see that, you know, the fabric is floating in this image. You are able to see the multi-layers fabric and the fact that the most outer layer is a chiffon or a sheer material. You can also see the radiant sunburst attachments that she made with sequins. The dress itself is actually one of her paintings that she turned into a print and put into a repeat for this dress.

Susima patterned her entire collection, another senior, on CLO and printed the patterns on her plotter to make twills and her final garments. Students were also introduced to Trudiform, which is a 3D body measurement software that allows users to scan their models using their iPhones. After the scan, she was able to print the patterns with a simple pen. The model was then printed before the scan. The scan is completed. The user receives an accurate measurement via an app, and then this can be transferred into a CLO avatar. As well as through the app, they will receive a 3D model in an OBJ. They will also get all of the measurements from their model that has been scanned.

So I don't know if you've had the pleasure to make these pictures. I hope you do. You're welcome. Thank you. To meet Jim Simon in the New York CLO office, but he and I worked together to take this 3D scan of the model and then turn it into a CLO avatar. So it worked out really wonderful. With her model scanned and now a CLO avatar, she could easily develop her designs and patterns with the correct fit for prototyping. This saved her a lot of time. She used the 3D pen avatar tool to intuitively perfect her styling lines and immediately turn them into patterns. This is a really fun feature.

One benefit of using CLO is that it can make a garment's life cycle more sustainable. Alyssa Boardman highlighted this feature in her CFDA scholarship application. And she stated the use of a virtual 3D modeling software such as CLO 3D significantly reduces the cost and the use of materials to draft and design this collection. Alyssa also designed and printed her own textiles with the help of CLO. This collection was developed in conjunction with her junior tailoring studio. Using the edit texture tool, Alyssa could easily design and print her own textiles with the help of CLO. Alyssa also designed and printed her own textiles with the help of CLO. This tool has been used to easily plan the most dynamic layout and scale of her print within her pattern pieces. So it gave her a lot of flexibility. And here is the front and back view of her final render for her tailored jacket.

I use CLO as a primary design tool for to design a customer outside the class. This class in addition to plants, mix of different types of waste pouring. So my students write sounds and make does not require pouring. So really piled up the hyvin strange details, acia final Artemis capsule collection that they designed. We also used the Oculus Quest VR to import their CLO models and Gravity Sketch, another program used for 3D modeling. And this is where students created some environments for their final presentation.

So a little bit about the class. NASA's Artemis Luna mission aims to return U.S. astronauts to the moon for the first time since 1972. So the students were briefed to design an in-ship gender-neutral wardrobe for astronauts that would be functional, comfortable, sustainable, breathable, aesthetically pleasing, of course, and easy to clean and able to endure a mission to the moon.

So here's one of our students, Aventica. She drew inspiration for her color story from the Aurora Borealis. And she found an iridescent fabric that was perfect for this in CLO Connect. And it rendered extremely well. For her capsule collection, Aventica, an ID student, incorporated ribbed joints for increased mobility, fabric loops in critical areas to hook sensors onto the garment, and hems that doubled as pockets. All these are very functional-oriented that you must have if you are in a microgravity system.

Alex, whose work that we had seen earlier, first learned CLO in Pack Your Bags. She was a junior at the time. Her final renders, her Artemis collection, and she focused on comfort. She used a lot of cut-and-sew knit fabrics and played with some really soft pastel colors, as well as a pop of red. So again, we can see and appreciate her signature rendering technique. That's great. So that has taken from an animation still frame. She also imported an HDRI file of a galaxy to use in her background for her CLO render. So if I click one more time, this should start the animation. There we go.

This fashion revolution, creating digital fashion for the Metaverse, was a class that I wrote and taught. It was a one-week workshop that I taught to middle and high school students in Shanghai and Beijing in the summer of 2023. So CLO was the main design tool for the students to create their own avatars for the Metaverse. They learned all about the Metaverse as well. The students were also introduced to AI texting. They were also introduced to AI text-to-image apps to help inspire their designs. So I took the liberty of putting the students' names along with their ages on the artwork that we're looking at here. So oddly and interestingly enough, the younger students, ages 11, 12, and 13, picked up the program faster than the 15- to the 18-year-olds. So given the one-week timeframe, I allowed students to download free CLO garments from the CLO Connect store as a starting point to then make their own designs and manipulations. They use the Edit Style Line tool as a way in making adjustments, as well as the modular library and the 3D pen tools to develop their designs.

At the age of 13, Gary got called in. He said, he was creative with the internal line tool to reshape his garments, and he had fun with the novelty fabrics he downloaded from CLO Connect. I was impressed with the students' outcomes and their abilities to navigate and use CLO all in the course of one week.

Michael Lai, the RISD NASA coordinator, designed and made this analog MS-1 Mars prototype spacesuit. In 2019, he asked me to pattern his spacesuit in CLO so we could make a few more prototypes for testing in a new design. So we used the CLO patterns as a starting point for a new design for a spacesuit. And we did this in the summer of 2023. And then last summer, 2024, we formed a new company. We formed a new company called XS3, which NASA has contracted us to make simulation spacesuits of their XEMU suits. So this is what the suit looked like in pattern pieces. I haven't counted up how many pattern pieces there are, but there are definitely a few hundred.

This work inspired me to teach and propose a class as a RISD elective, open to all students, called NASA Spacesuits Reimagined and Redesigned, which I'm currently teaching right now. So again, I'm using CLO as the primary design tool for the students to develop their design concepts. Now I'm going to hand this over to Joy.

Great. Thank you, Catherine. I'm Joy Kobe, and I came to using CLO3D through the research that I lead at RISD. But for the past few years, I've guided the work of the virtual textiles research group at RISD, which was founded in 2016 by members of the textiles department, as well as computer scientists at Cornell and Stanford. I've worked mostly with textile students, but have involved those in furniture, graphic design, sculpture, and also industrial design.

So I'll be talking about two main research threads that we've pursued and ways in which we've benefited from CLO3D. I thought it was a stroke of genius that Catherine came up with a title for our presentation, and that unstitched is not only a catchall for a lot of our visual output, but often functions as the inspiration for our work. And the motivation for both the chair that you see, which is a self-shaping textile, and the shoe, which is a 3D woven textile, was really to push what a textile could be. And in fact, each comes off the loom as a single textile, and with minimal finishing and certainly no stitching, it becomes the designed woven object.

So the first thread started at the height of the pandemic. So as a way to revive ourselves as a research group, after the deadening effects of lockdown, we were creating these complex woven fabrics, complex both in structure, as well as sensorily, in that they invited complex tactile interaction. So these woven textiles all have some context, of active yarn. So a material that strongly tends towards shrinkage, like elastomeric, even wool, or stiffness, like linen, or other physical behavior. So most of these come off the loom still in this rectangular form, but when activated by heat or moisture will take on these complex forms.

And the fundamental question in the field of self-shaping or active material is, how do we create a material that is more flexible, more flexible, is how do we, as designers, can harness these forces and get specific outcomes. So as many of you know, weaving these fabrics can be very time, material and labor intensive. So we wanted to understand what the fabric behavior would be in a visually intuitive way before actually making them. So our first cut was to use grasshopper for rhino, which was a tool that we were familiar with within the institution, to sketch examples of self-shaping fabrics as 3D modeled surfaces with shrinking and stiffness regions.

But this was also our first foray into CLO3D, trying to achieve the kind of behavior we were seeing from trial and error physical sampling, like boundary distortion, crumpling, pleating, and bubbling. And here we used really seamed pattern pieces as a stand-in for specifying regions with different shrinking and stiffness rates. And because these textiles undergo significant surface change from its rectangular state, it was extremely useful to be able to visualize this shape change in applications such as on a chair frame. And with the added confidence of these visualizations, and simulation tools, we could then scale to full scale prototyping, confident that the shrinkage when heated would result in a good fit for the prefabricated chair frame, and that the localized textures would serve their intended purpose.

And we were interested in practical applications of these textiles, but also curious about what we could learn from just observing and interacting with them. So much of the information we gather about an object, its weight, stiffness, smoothness, comes from sensing how it changes when we make these slight hand movements. If I rest on this fabric, will it flatten under my weight or spring back when I get up? We're interested in not just the final form of the textile after the shape change has taken place, but all of these additional possible states. And the sensory experience is both about the behavior and the application.

Moreover, seeing the textile form into a texture, its final relaxed state, as we know from seeing simulation of any textile in CLO, contributes to the sensory experience. So since our textiles had these very pronounced surface textures, communicating these sensory qualities in a virtual environment without feel also naturally brought us to the world of digital materials. Designing digital materials, PBRs that are used often within CLO, is typically done either procedurally or using some kind of scanning. And presenting this work at the preeminent computer graphics conference SIGGRAPH in 2022, we were introduced to a new digital material capture solution brewing between HP and Adobe substance called HPZ Captus.

And this was a full circle moment for us as a research group, which really had its origins from one of our founders watching Brave back in 2012 and thinking, if the animators make these make-believe fabric look so convincing, surely these tools can benefit textile designers in their design process. And we were amongst the first to be able to use the Captus. This is, again, this digital material capture device. In its early stages, this is a collaboration between HP and Adobe, and it uses the hardware of the photometric scanning from HP integrated with the software of Adobe Substance Sampler. And going from an existing fabric sample, like this lacy knit swatch, to packaging it in a usable format in CLO took me about 10 minutes. And right now, it can't capture all of the material maps, but already we see the potential for having digital materials that are able to capture all of the material maps. And so, we've been able to capture all of the digital materials with much richer tactile properties built in.

So, this was also the central ambition for this project, in which we developed a collection of novel materials with highly specific sensory qualities that exist both digitally and physically. Notice this wasn't just digital twinning, but instead balancing realistic qualities with the imaginary and the emotional.

The next thread was work with the RISD museum's department of costume and textiles, and the museum textiles setting provided this ready-made testbed for the previous project's work, given that so much of the emotional draw of textiles and garments involves experience of wearing and touching. And the primary goal that we set out was to explore ways we might employ digital materials to enhance visitors' tactile understanding and sensory experience of garments in a museum gallery setting, especially those garments that cannot, for one reason or another, be shown on bodily form.

And this project made central use of CLO3D, and I'm thankful for the contributions of Catherine, as well as Jim and Lindsay LeFoune in the CLO New York team. So for this project, we specifically selected South Asian garments as our focus, and all of these pieces we chose are unstitched garments, in that they are both fabric lengths as well as garments that derive their volumetric form through wrapping or draping around the body. And like the textiles that you see here displayed on the walls of this recently mounted exhibition, the textiles that we selected would also be shown flat, so as not to stress these fragile textiles.

All of these textiles we chose were over 100 years old, and yet these textiles really come to life, as we know, as garments through folding, pleating, and tucking, which often is a leap too far for many museum goers' imagination if they were displayed flat on the wall. So this conversation with the museum started shortly before the CLO accreditation course that I was lucky enough to attend in August of 2023, and was able to end that week with a good sketch of one sari drape. And thanks to Jim and Lindsey, that sketch was refined significantly and became the proof of concept for this project.

So the sari has many different drapes, but a relatively small number of operations. And the strategy that I have found most effective is to break up the fabric length, where the standard length of a sari is between five and a half meters to as long as eight meters long, into smaller lengths devoted to one layer, and then to seam them together. The translation for most of these operations is fairly straightforward, with a couple of exceptions, like knotting and tucking, which I found of course possible to do within CLO, but it looked better with tacking or more securely sewing.

And these translations, while good enough for rendering, would require more adjustments on a completely different approach if we were to get a good animation. The result depicted in these stills shows the gap that still exists between rendering and animation. The substantial amount of fabric wrapped around the body created this heavy model with multiple layers. And while the simulated cloth properties could be adjusted to correct some of the bounce, the primary issue lay with the motion file used. You can see that the large stride of the model was still a little bit loose and uneven in its overall design. As a result, the animation's movement might not be as natural as when you imagine a simple demonstration of a fabric spring over a humanoid.

In the metadata of the model we see that, while silhouettes may not be always typical to one walking a runway, maybe not the everyday movements one might have while wearing a sari. And this is kind of an internal look. Notice here that this is what you see from a museum database, and that both in the display as well as the descriptions, none of the distinctive sensory properties that we chose, the fabrics for are really reflected in these. And it's probably the rare exhibition on textiles that can really communicate how a textile feels.

And increasingly as AI generation depends so much on textual and image description, or rather the richness of that, the ability to get the sensory description right on the database level seems more pressing. So we wanted to create a sensory rich database that showcases the breadth of these textile traditions. So for each of the selected fabrics, we created representations of them, again, using Adobe Substance 3D. We modeled these 3D assets in application and furnished a description that alludes to the sensory experience of interacting with these textiles.

And as many of us know, so much of the sensory experience also comes from understanding the process. Looking at the back of this textile, this is called a bag fulcari, which is a nearly extinct extraordinary embroidery technique from Punjab area where the back of the fabric not only is beautiful in itself, but tells us so much about the process of making it. And as we move forward, we can see that the fabric that is being used is not only designed to be used as a kind of display, but also as a kind of display for the user to see what the fabric is doing as well. And using digital materials, we could showcase both sides of the fabrics, which is not easily done in a display behind glass.

And substance materials or PBR materials in general, but substance materials can be easily brought into CLO. And for the ones that we design procedurally, amongst the South Asian collection, we had some extraordinary fabrics made using the bandhani technique. This is commonly practiced in the western Indian states of Gujarat and Rajasthan. In this process, parts of the textiles are tied into knots with yarn to resist the absorption of the dye, resulting in these spotted patterns. This finished fabric is highly textured and, in this case, very lightweight and vibrantly colored. But modeling the feel of bandhani was challenging. The attempts to create a digital material were not so successful, it really came in looking quite flat, possibly because the knots are so dense that what gets picked up is a uniform height, which resulted in a digital material that looks thick and monolithic.

So what seemed to work better was to generate the pattern of knots, in this case, just using a circle packing technique in Rhino and Grasshopper, and then to apply elastic for the knot circles. It did become a very heavy model, but Catherine was able to get it to render. And you can see that what came out really came out as looking quite light. I think it reflects the lightweight feel of the fabric.

Thank you. And this work culminated in an exhibition at the RISD Museum called Sensory Silhouettes, which just ended its six-month run not too long ago. But thanks to the technical support I received from CLO3D for my research, I very recently started using CLO3D as a teaching tool and will be happy to report on how that has gone at the end of this school year.

Thank you very much.

You're very welcome.

chunks.content: ## Introduction to Stitched and Unstitched Apparel Design Using CLO 3D This section introduces the presenters and outlines the focus of the presentation on stitched and unstitched design workflows using CLO 3D, a prominent 3D garment visualization software. It highlights student projects that demonstrate the application of CLO for apparel design, pattern making, textile printing, and sustainable fashion development. - Catherine Andreuzzi, a professor at Rhode Island School of Design (RISD) in the apparel design department, presented alongside Joy Kobe from RISD’s textiles department. - The presentation was originally given at the New York CLO Summit and covers both stitched (apparel) and unstitched (textiles) workflows. ### Student Projects Using CLO 3D - **Alexandra Debler** designed a senior thesis collection inspired by occult and tarot themes, using CLO to develop intricate beading designs depicting moon phases on a jacket back. - Alexandra used CLO’s animation feature to find ideal fabric movement, freezing frames for final renders. Her work showcased multi-layered fabrics including sheer chiffon and sequin sunburst embellishments. - **Susima** patterned an entire collection in CLO, printing twill patterns with a plotter. The process included scanning models with Trudiform, a 3D body measurement software using iPhone scans, which generated accurate measurements and OBJ files transferrable into CLO avatars. - Using scanned avatars accelerated fit and prototyping, with CLO’s 3D pen avatar tool allowing intuitive refinement of styling lines into patterns. ### Sustainability and Textile Design - CLO reduces material waste and cost by enabling virtual 3D modeling, as highlighted by student Alyssa Boardman in her CFDA scholarship application. - Alyssa used CLO’s edit texture tool to design and print custom textiles, optimizing print layout and scale within pattern pieces. - Final renders demonstrated tailored garments with digital textile prints. ### Integration of VR and 3D Modeling Software - Students imported CLO models into Oculus Quest VR and Gravity Sketch to create immersive environments for presentations. - The Artemis Luna mission brief inspired a gender-neutral, functional, sustainable astronaut wardrobe. - Student **Aventica** designed a collection with features like ribbed joints for mobility, fabric loops for sensor attachment, and multifunctional hems, using iridescent fabrics sourced from CLO Connect. - Alexandra’s Artemis collection emphasized comfort with knit fabrics and pastel colors, rendered with HDRI galaxy backgrounds. ### Digital Fashion and Metaverse Design - Catherine taught a one-week workshop for middle and high school students in Shanghai and Beijing focused on digital fashion creation for the Metaverse using CLO. - Students were introduced to AI text-to-image tools to inspire designs. - Younger students (ages 11-13) adapted faster to CLO than older teens. - Students used CLO Connect’s free garments as templates, modifying designs with the Edit Style Line tool, modular libraries, and 3D pen tools. - Example: 13-year-old Gary creatively used internal line tools and novelty fabrics to reshape garments. ### NASA Spacesuit Prototyping with CLO - Michael Lai, RISD’s NASA coordinator, designed an analog MS-1 Mars prototype spacesuit in 2019.

chunks.content: - Students were introduced to AI text-to-image tools to inspire designs. - Younger students (ages 11-13) adapted faster to CLO than older teens. - Students used CLO Connect’s free garments as templates, modifying designs with the Edit Style Line tool, modular libraries, and 3D pen tools. - Example: 13-year-old Gary creatively used internal line tools and novelty fabrics to reshape garments. ### NASA Spacesuit Prototyping with CLO - Michael Lai, RISD’s NASA coordinator, designed an analog MS-1 Mars prototype spacesuit in 2019. - Catherine patterned the spacesuit in CLO for prototype development and redesign in summer 2023. - In 2024, a startup called XS3 was formed to contract with NASA to produce simulation spacesuits for XEMU suits. - Spacesuit patterns comprised hundreds of pieces, illustrating CLO’s capacity to handle complex technical garments. - Catherine teaches a RISD elective “NASA Spacesuits Reimagined and Redesigned” using CLO as the primary design tool. --- ## Unstitched Textiles Research and Digital Material Innovation This section covers Joy Kobe’s research on unstitched textiles at RISD, focusing on self-shaping textiles, digital material capture, and museum applications. It explores the use of CLO 3D and complementary software to simulate complex textile behaviors and sensory experiences without stitching. ### Virtual Textiles Research Group and Self-Shaping Fabrics - Founded in 2016, the RISD Virtual Textiles Research Group includes textiles, furniture, graphic design, sculpture, and industrial design disciplines. - Research focuses on complex woven fabrics with active yarns exhibiting shrinkage or stiffness, which self-shape when activated by heat or moisture. - Self-shaping textiles challenge designers to harness forces like shrinkage and stiffness for specific 3D outcomes. - Weaving these fabrics is material- and labor-intensive, motivating virtual simulation before production. - Initial simulations used Rhino’s Grasshopper to model shrinkage and stiffness regions as 3D surfaces. - CLO 3D enabled visualization of boundary distortions, crumpling, pleating, and bubbling in textile behavior, using seamed pattern pieces to represent different material zones. - Visualizing textile deformation on prefabricated objects (e.g., chair frames) improved confidence in scaling from virtual to physical prototypes. - The research emphasized not only final textile forms but also intermediate states and tactile interactions, important for sensory experience. ### Digital Materials and Photometric Scanning - The team explored digital material design using Physically Based Rendering (PBR) materials in CLO. - At SIGGRAPH 2022, they accessed HPZ Captus, a photometric scanning device developed by HP and Adobe Substance, to capture digital materials from real fabric samples. - The device integrates HP’s scanning hardware with Adobe Substance Sampler software. - Digital material capture from fabric to CLO-ready asset took approximately 10 minutes. - Current limitations include partial capture of material maps, but the technology shows promise for richer tactile digital materials. - The project aimed to create novel textile collections balancing realistic sensory properties with imaginative and emotional qualities, going beyond simple digital twinning. ### Museum Project: Enhancing Textile Sensory Experience Digitally - Collaboration with RISD Museum’s Costume and Textiles department focused on South Asian unstitched garments over 100 years old.

chunks.content: - Digital material capture from fabric to CLO-ready asset took approximately 10 minutes. - Current limitations include partial capture of material maps, but the technology shows promise for richer tactile digital materials. - The project aimed to create novel textile collections balancing realistic sensory properties with imaginative and emotional qualities, going beyond simple digital twinning. ### Museum Project: Enhancing Textile Sensory Experience Digitally - Collaboration with RISD Museum’s Costume and Textiles department focused on South Asian unstitched garments over 100 years old. - These textiles derive form through wrapping and draping rather than stitching, and are fragile, typically displayed flat. - The project used CLO 3D to digitally drape and render these textiles, enabling new ways to communicate their sensory and volumetric qualities without physical handling. - A sari drape was digitally sketched and refined with CLO New York staff, serving as proof of concept. - Saris (5.5 to 8 meters long) were digitally segmented and seamed to replicate layering and draping processes. - Some operations like knotting and tucking were simulated but required secure tacking or sewing in CLO for realism. - Challenges remain in animation smoothness due to heavy layered fabric and motion file limitations. - Metadata and museum descriptions currently lack detailed sensory information, which is critical for digital interpretation and AI-driven content generation. - The project created a sensory-rich digital database with 3D assets and descriptive text capturing tactile qualities of textiles. ### Specific Textile Case Studies - Example: Bag Fulcari embroidery from Punjab, a nearly extinct technique with highly detailed back embroidery revealing the making process. - Digital materials enabled visualization of both fabric sides, a challenge for physical museum displays. - Bandhani fabric (tie-dye technique from Gujarat and Rajasthan) presented challenges for digital material representation. - Attempts to replicate knot textures procedurally produced flat, monolithic digital materials. - A workaround involved generating knot patterns with circle packing in Rhino/Grasshopper and applying elastic properties. - The resulting CLO render appeared visually light and conveyed the fabric’s tactile qualities despite a heavy model. ### Exhibition and Teaching - The project culminated in the RISD Museum exhibition "Sensory Silhouettes," which ran for six months. - CLO 3D’s technical support was instrumental in this research. - Joy has recently incorporated CLO 3D as a teaching tool and plans to report on its educational outcomes. --- # Key Terms and Technologies - **CLO 3D**: Virtual apparel design and garment visualization software. - **Trudiform**: 3D body measurement app using iPhone scanning. - **3D Pen Avatar Tool**: CLO feature for drawing and adjusting style lines directly on avatars. - **Oculus Quest VR**: Virtual reality headset used for immersive design presentations. - **Gravity Sketch**: 3D modeling software used alongside CLO. - **HDRI (High Dynamic Range Imaging)**: Used to create realistic backgrounds in CLO renders. - **AI Text-to-Image Apps**: Artificial intelligence tools generating images from textual prompts. - **XS3**: Company contracted by NASA to produce simulation spacesuits. - **Virtual Textiles Research Group**: RISD interdisciplinary team exploring innovative textile design.

chunks.content: - **3D Pen Avatar Tool**: CLO feature for drawing and adjusting style lines directly on avatars. - **Oculus Quest VR**: Virtual reality headset used for immersive design presentations. - **Gravity Sketch**: 3D modeling software used alongside CLO. - **HDRI (High Dynamic Range Imaging)**: Used to create realistic backgrounds in CLO renders. - **AI Text-to-Image Apps**: Artificial intelligence tools generating images from textual prompts. - **XS3**: Company contracted by NASA to produce simulation spacesuits. - **Virtual Textiles Research Group**: RISD interdisciplinary team exploring innovative textile design. - **Physically Based Rendering (PBR)**: A material representation method for realistic digital textures. - **HPZ Captus**: Photometric scanner integrating HP hardware and Adobe Substance software for digital material capture. - **Bag Fulcari**: Traditional embroidered textile from Punjab. - **Bandhani**: Indian tie-dye textile technique. - **Grasshopper for Rhino**: Visual programming tool used for parametric design and textile modeling. --- # Summary This presentation showcases the integration of CLO 3D in both stitched and unstitched design realms, highlighting educational, research, and industrial applications. It illustrates how CLO facilitates sustainable fashion development, immersive virtual fashion experiences, complex technical garment prototyping (e.g., NASA spacesuits), and innovative textile research including self-shaping materials and sensory-rich digital representations for museum use. The collaboration between apparel and textile disciplines at RISD, supported by emerging digital material capture technologies, exemplifies the expanding role of 3D simulation in fashion and textile innovation.

The Artemis Luna mission brief inspired a gender-neutral, functional, sustainable astronaut wardrobe. - Student **Aventica** designed a collection with features like ribbed joints for mobility, fabric loops for sensor attachment, and multifunctional hems, using iridescent fabrics sourced from CLO Connect. - Alexandra’s Artemis collection emphasized comfort with knit fabrics and pastel colors, rendered with HDRI galaxy backgrounds. ### Digital Fashion and Metaverse Design - Catherine taught a one-week workshop for middle and high school students in Shanghai and Beijing focused on digital fashion creation for the Metaverse using CLO. - Students were introduced to AI text-to-image tools to inspire designs. - Younger students (ages 11-13) adapted faster to CLO than older teens. - Students used CLO Connect’s free garments as templates, modifying designs with the Edit Style Line tool, modular libraries, and 3D pen tools. - Example: 13-year-old Gary creatively used internal line tools and novelty fabrics to reshape garments. ### NASA Spacesuit Prototyping with CLO - Michael Lai, RISD’s NASA coordinator, designed an analog MS-1 Mars prototype spacesuit in 2019. - Catherine patterned the spacesuit in CLO for prototype development and redesign in summer 2023. - In 2024, a startup called XS3 was formed to contract with NASA to produce simulation spacesuits for XEMU suits. - Spacesuit patterns comprised hundreds of pieces, illustrating CLO’s capacity to handle complex technical garments. - Catherine teaches a RISD elective “NASA Spacesuits Reimagined and Redesigned” using CLO as the primary design tool. --- ## Unstitched Textiles Research and Digital Material Innovation This section covers Joy Kobe’s research on unstitched textiles at RISD, focusing on self-shaping textiles, digital material capture, and museum applications. It explores the use of CLO 3D and complementary software to simulate complex textile behaviors and sensory experiences without stitching. ### Virtual Textiles Research Group and Self-Shaping Fabrics - Founded in 2016, the RISD Virtual Textiles Research Group includes textiles, furniture, graphic design, sculpture, and industrial design disciplines. - Research focuses on complex woven fabrics with active yarns exhibiting shrinkage or stiffness, which self-shape when activated by heat or moisture. - Self-shaping textiles challenge designers to harness forces like shrinkage and stiffness for specific 3D outcomes. - Weaving these fabrics is material- and labor-intensive, motivating virtual simulation before production. - Initial simulations used Rhino’s Grasshopper to model shrinkage and stiffness regions as 3D surfaces. - CLO 3D enabled visualization of boundary distortions, crumpling, pleating, and bubbling in textile behavior, using seamed pattern pieces to represent different material zones. - Visualizing textile deformation on prefabricated objects (e.g., chair frames) improved confidence in scaling from virtual to physical prototypes. - The research emphasized not only final textile forms but also intermediate states and tactile interactions, important for sensory experience. ### Digital Materials and Photometric Scanning - The team explored digital material design using Physically Based Rendering (PBR) materials in CLO. - At SIGGRAPH 2022, they accessed HPZ Captus, a photometric scanning device developed by HP and Adobe Substance, to capture digital materials from real fabric samples. - The device integrates HP’s scanning hardware with Adobe Substance Sampler software. - Digital material capture from fabric to CLO-ready asset took approximately 10 minutes. - Current limitations include partial capture of material maps, but the technology shows promise for richer tactile digital materials. - The project aimed to create novel textile collections balancing realistic sensory properties with imaginative and emotional qualities, going beyond simple digital twinning. ### Museum Project: Enhancing Textile Sensory Experience Digitally - Collaboration with RISD Museum’s Costume and Textiles department focused on South Asian unstitched garments over 100 years old. - These textiles derive form through wrapping and draping rather than stitching, and are fragile, typically displayed flat. - The project used CLO 3D to digitally drape and render these textiles, enabling new ways to communicate their sensory and volumetric qualities without physical handling. - A sari drape was digitally sketched and refined with CLO New York staff, serving as proof of concept. - Saris (5.5 to 8 meters long) were digitally segmented and seamed to replicate layering and draping processes. - Some operations like knotting and tucking were simulated but required secure tacking or sewing in CLO for realism. - Challenges remain in animation smoothness due to heavy layered fabric and motion file limitations. - Metadata and museum descriptions currently lack detailed sensory information, which is critical for digital interpretation and AI-driven content generation. - The project created a sensory-rich digital database with 3D assets and descriptive text capturing tactile qualities of textiles. ### Specific Textile Case Studies - Example: Bag Fulcari embroidery from Punjab, a nearly extinct technique with highly detailed back embroidery revealing the making process. - Digital materials enabled visualization of both fabric sides, a challenge for physical museum displays. - Bandhani fabric (tie-dye technique from Gujarat and Rajasthan) presented challenges for digital material representation. - Attempts to replicate knot textures procedurally produced flat, monolithic digital materials. - A workaround involved generating knot patterns with circle packing in Rhino/Grasshopper and applying elastic properties. - The resulting CLO render appeared visually light and conveyed the fabric’s tactile qualities despite a heavy model. ### Exhibition and Teaching - The project culminated in the RISD Museum exhibition "Sensory Silhouettes," which ran for six months. - CLO 3D’s technical support was instrumental in this research. - Joy has recently incorporated CLO 3D as a teaching tool and plans to report on its educational outcomes. --- # Key Terms and Technologies - **CLO 3D**: Virtual apparel design and garment visualization software. - **Trudiform**: 3D body measurement app using iPhone scanning. - **3D Pen Avatar Tool**: CLO feature for drawing and adjusting style lines directly on avatars. - **Oculus Quest VR**: Virtual reality headset used for immersive design presentations. - **Gravity Sketch**: 3D modeling software used alongside CLO. - **HDRI (High Dynamic Range Imaging)**: Used to create realistic backgrounds in CLO renders. - **AI Text-to-Image Apps**: Artificial intelligence tools generating images from textual prompts. - **XS3**: Company contracted by NASA to produce simulation spacesuits. - **Virtual Textiles Research Group**: RISD interdisciplinary team exploring innovative textile design. - **Physically Based Rendering (PBR)**: A material representation method for realistic digital textures. - **HPZ Captus**: Photometric scanner integrating HP hardware and Adobe Substance software for digital material capture. - **Bag Fulcari**: Traditional embroidered textile from Punjab. - **Bandhani**: Indian tie-dye textile technique. - **Grasshopper for Rhino**: Visual programming tool used for parametric design and textile modeling. --- # Summary This presentation showcases the integration of CLO 3D in both stitched and unstitched design realms, highlighting educational, research, and industrial applications. It illustrates how CLO facilitates sustainable fashion development, immersive virtual fashion experiences, complex technical garment prototyping (e.g., NASA spacesuits), and innovative textile research including self-shaping materials and sensory-rich digital representations for museum use. The collaboration between apparel and textile disciplines at RISD, supported by emerging digital material capture technologies, exemplifies the expanding role of 3D simulation in fashion and textile innovation.
